headline: Nature's Antivenom: Scientists Learn from Snakes' Own Immunity
meta_description: Scientists are developing new antivenoms by studying how snakes naturally resist their own venom, offering hope to millions affected by snakebites annually.
summary_short: A groundbreaking approach to treating snakebites draws inspiration from an unexpected source: the snakes themselves and their built-in resistance to venom.
body:
Snakebite remains one of the world's most undertreated tropical diseases, affecting over one million people annually and causing approximately 100,000 deaths and 400,000 disabilities each year.

Now, scientists have discovered an elegant solution hidden in nature itself. By studying vipers, researchers noticed something remarkable: these snakes possess natural resistance to the hemorrhagic and lethal effects of their own venom. Rather than fighting against this biology, scientists are using it as a blueprint.

This approach represents a fundamental shift in how antivenoms are developed. Instead of relying solely on conventional methods, the new generation of treatments will be inspired by the immune mechanisms that allow snakes to survive their own toxins—turning predators into unlikely teachers in the fight against one of medicine's most neglected threats.
